A compass
options.rationale: A compass uses a permanent magnet.

options.content: A fridge door seal
options.rationale: That uses a permanent magnetic strip.

options.content: A bar magnet

explanation: An electric bell uses an electromagnet that switches on and off repeatedly.

stem: Why is an electromagnet, rather than a permanent magnet, used on a scrap-yard crane?

options.content: It can be switched off to release the load.
It attracts aluminium as well as iron.
It never needs any electricity.
It is always weaker, which is safer.

explanation: The crane must drop its load: switching off the current makes the soft-iron core lose its magnetism.

stem: Which of these uses needs a permanent magnet?

options.content: A relay
An electric bell
A circuit breaker
A compass needle

explanation: A compass needle must stay magnetised all the time, so it is a permanent magnet.

stem: The core of an electromagnet should be made of steel so that it keeps its magnetism.
explanation: The core should be soft iron, which loses its magnetism when the current stops; that is the whole point of an electromagnet.

stem: Match each device with how it uses magnetism.

right.content: Lifts iron and releases it when the current is switched off
A magnetised needle lines up with the Earth's field
A small current in a coil switches a separate circuit
An armature is repeatedly attracted and released

explanation: Relay: switching. Bell: armature on and off. Crane: lift and release. Compass: alignment.

stem: In an electric bell, why does the armature keep moving back and forth while the bell push is pressed?

options.content: The current is alternating, so the magnet keeps reversing.
options.rationale: Bells usually run on d.c.; the make-and-break contact does the switching.

options.content: Pulling the armature breaks the circuit; a spring then remakes it.
The hammer bounces off the gong and back again.
The gong pushes the armature back each time with a magnetic force of its own.
options.rationale: The gong is not a magnet.

explanation: The make-and-break contact switches the electromagnet off each time the armature moves, so the cycle repeats.
hints: What happens to the circuit when the armature moves towards the electromagnet?

stem: What is the main purpose of a relay?

options.content: To increase the voltage of a supply for a large load
To store electrical energy until the circuit it controls needs it
options.rationale: A relay is a switch, not a store.

options.content: To let a small current switch a separate large-current circuit
To change a.c. into d.c. for the circuit it switches

explanation: A relay uses a small current in its coil to close (or open) contacts in another circuit.

stem: At a recycling plant, steel cans are separated from aluminium cans using a large magnet. Why does this work?

options.content: Aluminium is heavier than steel.
Steel is a better electrical conductor.
options.rationale: Magnetic separation does not depend on conduction.

options.content: Aluminium is magnetic but steel is not.
options.rationale: It is the other way round.

options.content: Steel is magnetic but aluminium is not.

explanation: The magnet attracts the steel cans and leaves the non-magnetic aluminium cans behind.

stem: Why is the armature of an electric bell made of soft iron?

options.content: It is a good electrical conductor for the contacts.
It demagnetises at once, so it is released when current stops.
It is a permanent magnet that keeps its strength.
It is non-magnetic, so it springs back freely each time.
options.rationale: It must be attracted by the electromagnet.

explanation: A steel armature would stay magnetised and stick to the electromagnet; soft iron lets go at once.
hints: What must happen to the armature when the current stops?

stem: Select **all** the devices that contain a permanent magnet.

options.content: The core of a scrap-yard lifting magnet
A loudspeaker
A bicycle dynamo
A compass
The core of an electric bell's electromagnet
The core of a relay coil

explanation: Loudspeakers, dynamos and compasses use permanent magnets; electromagnet cores are soft iron.
hints: Which devices need a magnetic field all the time?

stem: Name the type of magnet that can be switched on and off.
explanation: An electromagnet is magnetised only while a current flows.

stem: A car's key switch operates the starter motor through a relay.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Why is a relay used instead of a key switch that carries the starter current directly?

options.content: A relay increases the current reaching the starter motor.
options.rationale: It switches the current; it does not increase it.

options.content: The starter motor needs a.c., which the relay supplies.
The key carries a small current; the huge current uses thick cables.
Relays are cheaper to fit than the long lengths of thick copper cable.

parts.explanation: The relay keeps the large current out of the dashboard switch and its thin wiring.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe what happens inside the relay when the key switch is turned.

points.description: A small current flows through the relay coil and magnetises its soft-iron core
The core attracts the armature, which closes the contacts and completes the starter-motor circuit

explanation: A small coil current magnetises the relay core, which pulls the armature and closes the high-current contacts.
hints: A relay is an electromagnet that operates a switch.
